pll1d44c1-d1e3506.summary: Asks whether God can make something better than he makes it.

pll1d44c1-d1e3512.summary: Reports the 'searchers' who say God cannot make things better, or he would be envious and not supremely good, arguing by analogy.

pll1d44c1-d1e3515.summary: Gives their analogy from Augustine's 83 Questions: God begot an equal Son, since if he willed and could not he would be weak, if he could and would not envious. Lombard says the analogy fails: the Son is from God's substance, so not begetting an equal would be envy, but other things, not from his substance, can be made better.
claims: The Son, being from God's substance, had to be equal.
Creatures, not from God's substance, can be made better.

pll1d44c1-d1e3535.summary: Asks them why a thing or the whole universe cannot be better: if because supremely good, lacking no perfection, the creature would equal the Creator; if because it cannot receive more good, that inability is a defect, and it could be made better if made capable, which its maker can do. So God can make things better.
claims: If creation were supremely good, it would equal God.
Inability to receive more good is a defect.

pll1d44c1-d1e3538.summary: Cites Augustine on Genesis: God could have made man neither able nor willing to sin, and who doubts that would have been better?
claims: God could have made a better human.

pll1d44c1-d1e3558.summary: Concludes that God can make other things than he makes and make what he makes better.
claims: God can make other and better things.

pll1d44c1-d1e3561.summary: Asks whether God can make what he makes in another or better way. If the mode refers to the maker's wisdom, it can be neither other nor better.
claims: God's mode of working, as his wisdom, cannot be better.

pll1d44c1-d1e3567.summary: Explains: God cannot act with other or greater wisdom; but if the mode refers to the thing made, there can be another and better mode, since God can give some things a better mode of being and others a different one.
claims: God can give creatures a better mode of being.

pll1d44c1-d1e3570.summary: Cites De Trinitate XIII: another mode of our liberation was possible to God, but none more fitting for healing our misery. So God can make some things in a better way, some equally good, some less good, the mode referring to the creature's quality, not the Creator's wisdom.
claims: Another mode of redemption was possible, but none more fitting.
Modes of creatures can be better, equal, or worse.

pl-l1d44c1.summary: Asks whether God can make things better than he makes them. The 'searchers' say no, or he would be envious, arguing from Augustine: God begot an equal Son, since if he could and would not he would be envious. Lombard rejects the analogy: the Son is from God's substance, but other things are not. He asks them why the universe cannot be better: if because it is supremely good, the creature would equal the Creator; if because it cannot receive more good, that is a defect, which its maker can remedy. Augustine: God could have made man unable to sin, and that would have been better. So God can make other and better things. Regarding the mode of action, if referred to the maker's wisdom, it cannot be other or better; if referred to the thing made, it can, since, as Augustine says, another mode of our liberation was possible, though none more fitting.
claims: God can make things better than he makes them.
The argument from the begetting of an equal Son does not apply to creatures, which are not from God's substance.
If creation were supremely good, the creature would equal the Creator.
A creature's inability to receive greater good is a defect God can remedy.
God could have made man unable to sin, which would be better.
God cannot act with greater wisdom, but can give things a better mode of being.
Another mode of our liberation was possible, though none more fitting.
